blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Rotational motion describes the movement of an object around an axis. Key quantities include:

  • Angular Displacement (θ): The angle through which an object rotates.
  • Angular Velocity (ω): The rate at which an object rotates, measured in radians per second.
  • Angular Acceleration (α): The rate of change of angular velocity with time.
  • Torque (τ): The force that causes an object to rotate, similar to force in linear motion.
  • Moment of Inertia (I): An object's resistance to change state of its in rotational motion, like mass in linear motion.

rows: (1) If angular acceleration is 0,$\omega$=Constant and $\theta=\omega t$

(2) If acceleration a =constant (a) $\mathrm{s}=\frac{(\mathrm{u}+\mathrm{v})}{2} \mathrm{t}$(b) $\mathrm{v}=\mathrm{u}+\mathrm{at}$(c) $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2$(d) $\mathrm{v}^2=\mathrm{u}^2+2 \mathrm{as}$(e) $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}^{\mathrm{th}}}=\mathrm{u}+\frac{\mathrm{a}}{2}(2 \mathrm{n}-1)$

(2) If angular Acceleration $\alpha$=Constant(a) $\theta=\frac{\left(\omega_0+\omega\right)}{2} \mathrm{t}$(b) $\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t$(c) $\theta=\omega_0 t+\frac{1}{2} \alpha t^2$(d) $\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2 \alpha \theta$(e) $\theta_{\mathrm{n}^{th}}=\omega_0+\frac{\alpha}{2}(2 \mathrm{n}-1)$
(3) If angular acceleration is not constant$\begin{aligned} & \omega=\frac{d \theta}{d t} \\ & a=\frac{d \omega}{d t}=\frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2}=\omega \frac{d \omega}{d \theta} \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question:
A wheel is rotating with angular velocity 2 rad/s. It is subjected to a uniform angular acceleration
2.0 rad/s2.

(a) What angular velocity does the wheel acquire after 10 s?

(b) How many revolutions will it make in this time interval?
blocks.answer:
The wheel is in uniform angular acceleration, Hence

(a)  $\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t$

$\omega=2+2 \times 10=22 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$

(b)  $\theta=\frac{1}{2}\left(\omega_{\circ}+\omega\right) \mathrm{t}$

$\theta=\frac{1}{2}(2+22) 10=120 \mathrm{rad}$

In one revolution, the wheel rotates through 2$\pi$ radians. Therefore the number of complete revolutions n is,

$\mathrm{n}=\frac{\theta}{2 \pi}=\frac{120}{2 \pi} \approx 19$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Moment of Inertia: The measure of the property by virtue of which a body revolving about an axis opposes any change in state of its rotational motion is known as moment of inertia.

The moment of inertia of a particle with respect to an axis of rotation is equal to the product of its mass and the square of its perpendicular distance from the rotational axis.

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{mr}^2$, $r=$Perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation

Moment of Inertia for Discrete System of Particles:

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{r}_1^2+\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{r}_2^2+\mathrm{m}_3 \mathrm{r}_3^2+\ldots . .=\sum \mathrm{mr}^2$

Moment of inertia depends on :

(a) Mass of the body

(b) Mass distribution of the body

(c) Position of axis of rotation

Moment of inertia does not depend on :-

(a) angular velocity

(b) angular acceleration

(c) torque

(d) angular momentum

Unit : SI : kg–m2,  CGS : g–cm2 ,  Dimension : [M1L2T0]

Note: As the distance of mass increases from the rotational axis, the moment of inertia increases.

Moment of inertia for continuous mass distributions:

$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{AB}}=\int \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{dm}$

Note: Moment of inertia of two or more than two bodies can be added or subtracted only when all moment of inertia are written with respect to same axis.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Perpendicular Axis Theorem: The moment of inertia (MOI) of a plane lamina about an axis perpendicular to its plane is equal to the sum of its moments of inertia about any two mutually perpendicular axes in its own plane intersecting each other at the point through which the perpendicular axis passes.

$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{z}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{y}}$

  • The theorem is only valid for thin and flat (Planar Objects) , two-dimensional objects that lie in a plane (e.g., disks, thin plates).
  • The two axes x and y must lie within the plane of the object, and the third axis z is perpendicular to that plane.
Parallel Axis Theorem: Moment of inertia of a body about any axis is equal to the moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through the centre of mass plus product of mass of the body and the square of the distance between these two parallel axes.

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{CM}}+\mathrm{Md}^2$

  • Theorem is valid for all type of bodies.
Radius of Gyration: The Radius of gyration of a body is the distance from axis of rotation, the square of this distance when multiplied by the mass of body then it gives the moment of inertia of the body $(I=MK^{2})$ about same axis of rotation.

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{MK}^2$

$\mathrm{K}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{M}}}$

• K has no meaning without axis of rotation.

Radius of gyration depends on

(1) axis of rotation

(2) distribution of mass of body

Radius of gyration does not depend on

(1) Mass of the body

(2) Angular quantities (angular displacement, angular velocity etc

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Calculate the moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass M and radius R about the axis passing through its diameter.
blocks.answer:
Let us consider the x-axis to be the diameter about which the moment of inertia of the disc has to be calculated. Say, the moment of inertia of the disc about the axis, Ix = I.

It is clear that the y-axis is also a diameter similar to the x-axis. So, Iy = Ix = I.

We also know that the moment of inertia of the disc about the centroidal axis is,

$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{z}}=\frac{\mathrm{MR}^2}{2}$

From perpendicular axis theorem,

$\mathrm{I}_z=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{y}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{x}}=2 \mathrm{I}$

$2 \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{MR}^2}{2} \Rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{MR}^2}{2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{MR}^2}{4}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Moment of a Force-Torque

  • It is the physical quantity which is responsible for change in state of rotation. It is essential for producing turning / toppling phenomena.
  • For producing torque the force is required & it is product of force and perpendicular distance of line of action of force.
OB is the perpendicular distance of line of action from point about O which is $ r ~ sin\theta$

$\tau=\mathrm{Fr} \sin \theta$

$\vec{\tau}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}$

$\vec{F}=$Force applied

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}$= position vector of the point of application of force w.r.t the point about which we want to determine the torque

1. It is an axial vector i.e. its direction is always perpendicular to the plane containing vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}$ and $\vec{F}$.

2. It's direction is determined by right hand thumb rule.

3. Let Positive sign to all torques acting to turn a body anti clockwise and a negative to all torque tending to turn it clockwise.

Unit of torque : N-m (same as that of work or energy)

Dimensions of torque : [ML2T–2]

Note: Unit of torque (N-m) cannot be written as joule, because joule is used specifically for work or energy.

Couple of forces :when two forces of equal magnitude act on different points and in opposite directions with distinct lines of action these force form a couple. This couple tries to rotate body.

Moment of Force,

$\tau=\mathrm{Fr} \sin \theta=\mathrm{Fb}$

$\tau=\text { constant } \Rightarrow \mathrm{Frsin} \theta=\text { constant } \Rightarrow F=\frac{\text { constant }}{r \sin \theta}$

Longer the arm and greater the value of sin $\theta$, lesser will be the force required for producing desired rotational effect. This fact explains why it is much easier to rotate a body about a given axis when the force is applied at maximum distance from the axis of rotation and normal to the arm.

Important points

1. If line of action of a force passes through point O, then Torque of this force about point O will be zero.

2.If a force is acting parallel to the axis of rotation, then it’s rotational effect about that axis will be zero.

3.If line of action of a force passes through axis of rotation, then it’s rotational effect (Torque) about that axis of rotation will be zero.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies:

Equilibrium refers to the state where the body is not experiencing any net force or net torque.

Two types of equilibrium in rigid bodies:

1.Translational Equilibrium: This occurs when the sum of all external forces acting on the body is zero,

$\sum \vec{F}= \vec0$

Note: Translational equilibrium ensures that the object does not experience any linear acceleration.

2.Rotational Equilibrium: This occurs when the sum of all external torques acting on the body about any axis is zero.

$\sum \vec \tau= \vec0$

Note: Rotational equilibrium ensures that the object does not experience any angular acceleration.

Examples of Rotational Equilibrium : Seesaw ,Balance Scale

Relation Between torque and Angular Acceleration

$\tau_{\text {net }}=\mathrm{I} \alpha$

Note: This equation is valid only for fixed axis.

Rotating Pulley

Angular acceleration for heavy pulley

Friction is present between the string and pulley i.e. There is no relative slipping between string and pulley.

No slipping

$\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {string }}\right)_p=\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {pulley }}\right)_p$

$\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{R} \alpha \Rightarrow \quad \alpha=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{R}}$

$\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~g}}{\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2+\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{R}^2}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\frac{\text { Net force along string }}{\left(\text { total mass of blocks }+\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{R}^2}\right)}$

Toppling:

In many situations an external force is applied to a body to cause it to slide along a surface. In certain cases, the body may tip over before sliding. This is known as toppling.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Angular momentum of a Particle : Angular momentum of a body about a given axis is the product of its linear momentum and perpendicular distance of line of action of linear momentum vector from the point of rotation.

Angular momentum = Linear momentum × Perpendicular distance of line of action of momentum from the point of rotation

$\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{mv} \times \mathrm{r} \sin \theta \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~L}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}$

Here$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}=$ angular momentum of a moving particle about point O

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}$ is the is the linear momentum of the particle

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}$ is the position vector of the particle regarding the point.

Unit :  kg – m2/sec

Dimension : [ML2T–1]

Angular momentum is an axial vector and it is also defined as moment of linear momentum.

• If line of motion of a particle passes through point 'O', then angular momentum about point O will be zero.

$\begin{aligned} &(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}})_0=0\\ &\text { Because } r_{\perp}=0 \end{aligned}$

Direction of angular momentum: Determined by Right hand thumb rule

Angular momentum of a rigid body rotating about fixed axis:

$L = I \omega$

Angular momentum of combined rotation and translation

Angular momentum of the body about a point P outside the body is given by,

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_p=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{cm}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_{\mathrm{cm}}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_p=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{cm}} \vec{\omega}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{cm}}$

Note: Always consider positive and negative sign while calculating these values.

Newton's 2nd Law in Rotation: It states that net external Torque acting on a system about any point O (or axis) is equal to rate of change of angular momentum of system about any point O (or axis).

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad\left(\vec{\tau}_{\text {ext }}\right)_0=\frac{d L_0}{d t} \quad \text { Also, } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_0=\mathrm{I}_0 \vec{\omega} \\ & \text { So, }\left(\vec{\tau}_{\text {ext }}\right)_0=\frac{d\left(I_0 \vec{\omega}\right)}{d t}=I_0 \frac{d \vec{\omega}}{d t}=I_0 \vec{\alpha} \end{aligned}$

$\vec{\tau}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\Delta \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{f}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\mathrm{t}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Conservation of Angular Momentum (COAM): If the resultant external torque acting on a system is zero then the total angular momentum of the system remains constant.

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau}_{\mathrm{cxt}} &= \frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dL}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ \text{If } \bar{\tau}_{\mathrm{ext}} &= 0 \Rightarrow \frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dL}}}{\mathrm{dt}} = 0 \\ &\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}} \text{ is constant} \\ &\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{i}}} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{f}}} \end{aligned}$

$I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$

Rotational kinetic Energy:

The energy possessed due to rotational motion of a body is known as rotational kinetic energy.

It is a scalar quantity.

$\mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_2 \mathrm{v}_2^2+\ldots=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{r}_1^2+\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{r}_2^2+\ldots\right) \omega^2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2$

Relation between angular momentum and Rotational kinetic energy:

$\mathrm{KE_{Rotation}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2$

$\mathrm{KE}_{\text {rotation }}=\frac{\mathrm{L}^2}{2 \mathrm{I}}$

Total kinetic energy in combined translation and rotation: If during rotation, the centre of mass of the rigid body undergoes translational motion, it will have both translational and rotational kinetic energy.

$\mathrm{K}_{\text {total }}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MV}_{\mathrm{C}}^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}} \omega^2$

Rotational power: The power associated with the work done by torque acting on a rotating body.

$P_r=\vec{\tau} \cdot \vec{\omega} .$

Work-Energy Theorem in Rotational motion: The change in the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid body equals the work done by external torques exerted on the body. This equation is analogous to equation corresponding to the work-energy theorem applicable for a particle.

Work done by the torque = Change in kinetic energy of rotation

$\mathrm{W}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega_2^2-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega_1^2$

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Rolling Motion:

When a body performs translatory motion as well as rotatory motion combinedly then it is said to undergo rolling motion.

Pure Rolling:

1.If the relative velocity of the point of contact of the rolling body with the surface is zero then it is known as pure rolling $v_{C M}=R \omega$

2. If a body is performing rolling then the velocity of any point of the body with respect to the surface is given by $\vec{v}=\overrightarrow{v_{C M}}+\vec{\omega} \times \vec{R}$

Total kinetic energy of a purely rolling objects:

$K \cdot E_{\text {total }}=\frac{1}{2} M V_c^2\left[1+\frac{K}{R^2}\right]$

$\frac{K \cdot E_{\text {total }}}{K \cdot E_{\text {trans }}}=\frac{K^2}{R^2}$

So value of $\left(\frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)$ is maximum for ring or hollow cylinder=1 and minimum for solid sphere$=\frac{2}{5}=0.4$

Rolling With Slipping:

When a body rolls on a surface under external force, the frictional force on the body (if any) will be static in nature, less than its limiting value. But if the object rolls with slipping the nature of friction should be kinetic in nature.

columns: Accelerated Pure Rolling,$a_{C O M}=\alpha R$

$V=\omega R$ (Initial),Static Friction whose values can lies between zero and $\mu$N  will act in backward direction.
Change in Kinetic Energy Due to Rolling$v_2>v_1$$=\frac{1}{2} m\left(1+\frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)\left(v_2^2-v_1^2\right)$

Rolling v/s Sliding$\begin{gathered} v_{\text {Rolling }}=\frac{V_{\text {sliding }}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{K^2}{R^2}}}, a_{\text {Rolling }}=\frac{a_{\text {Sliding }}}{1+\frac{K^2}{R^2}}, t_{\text {Rolling }}=t_{\text {sliding }} \sqrt{1+\frac{K^2}{R^2}} \\ v_{\text {Rolling }}<v_{\text {sliding }}, \quad a_{\text {Rolling }}<a_{\text {Sliding }}, \quad t_{\text {Rolling }}>t_{\text {Sliding }} \mid \end{gathered}$

So value of $\left(\frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)$ is maximum for ring or hollow cylinder=1 and minimum for solid sphere$=\frac{2}{5}=0.4$

Rolling With Slipping:

When a body rolls on a surface under external force, the frictional force on the body (if any) will be static in nature, less than its limiting value. But if the object rolls with slipping the nature of friction should be kinetic in nature.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Perpendicular Axis Theorem: The moment of inertia (MOI) of a plane lamina about an axis perpendicular to its plane is equal to the sum of its moments of inertia about any two mutually perpendicular axes in its own plane intersecting each other at the point through which the perpendicular axis passes.

$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{z}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{y}}$

  • The theorem is only valid for thin and flat (Planar Objects) , two-dimensional objects that lie in a plane (e.g., disks, thin plates).
  • The two axes x and y must lie within the plane of the object, and the third axis z is perpendicular to that plane.
Parallel Axis Theorem: Moment of inertia of a body about any axis is equal to the moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through the centre of mass plus product of mass of the body and the square of the distance between these two parallel axes.

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{CM}}+\mathrm{Md}^2$

  • Theorem is valid for all type of bodies.
Radius of Gyration: The Radius of gyration of a body is the distance from axis of rotation, the square of this distance when multiplied by the mass of body then it gives the moment of inertia of the body $(I=MK^{2})$ about same axis of rotation.

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{MK}^2$

$\mathrm{K}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{M}}}$

• K has no meaning without axis of rotation.

Radius of gyration depends on

(1) axis of rotation

(2) distribution of mass of body

Radius of gyration does not depend on

(1) Mass of the body

(2) Angular quantities (angular displacement, angular velocity etc

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Moment of a Force-Torque

  • It is the physical quantity which is responsible for change in state of rotation. It is essential for producing turning / toppling phenomena.
  • For producing torque the force is required & it is product of force and perpendicular distance of line of action of force.
OB is the perpendicular distance of line of action from point about O which is $ r ~ sin\theta$

$\tau=\mathrm{Fr} \sin \theta$

$\vec{\tau}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}$

$\vec{F}=$Force applied

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}$= position vector of the point of application of force w.r.t the point about which we want to determine the torque

1. It is an axial vector i.e. its direction is always perpendicular to the plane containing vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}$ and $\vec{F}$.

2. It's direction is determined by right hand thumb rule.

3. Let Positive sign to all torques acting to turn a body anti clockwise and a negative to all torque tending to turn it clockwise.

Unit of torque : N-m (same as that of work or energy)

Dimensions of torque : [ML2T–2]

Note: Unit of torque (N-m) cannot be written as joule, because joule is used specifically for work or energy.

Couple of forces :when two forces of equal magnitude act on different points and in opposite directions with distinct lines of action these force form a couple. This couple tries to rotate body.

Moment of Force,

$\tau=\mathrm{Fr} \sin \theta=\mathrm{Fb}$

$\tau=\text { constant } \Rightarrow \mathrm{Frsin} \theta=\text { constant } \Rightarrow F=\frac{\text { constant }}{r \sin \theta}$

Longer the arm and greater the value of sin $\theta$, lesser will be the force required for producing desired rotational effect. This fact explains why it is much easier to rotate a body about a given axis when the force is applied at maximum distance from the axis of rotation and normal to the arm.

Important points

1. If line of action of a force passes through point O, then Torque of this force about point O will be zero.

2.If a force is acting parallel to the axis of rotation, then it’s rotational effect about that axis will be zero.

3.If line of action of a force passes through axis of rotation, then it’s rotational effect (Torque) about that axis of rotation will be zero.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies:

Equilibrium refers to the state where the body is not experiencing any net force or net torque.

Two types of equilibrium in rigid bodies:

1.Translational Equilibrium: This occurs when the sum of all external forces acting on the body is zero,

$\sum \vec{F}= \vec0$

Note: Translational equilibrium ensures that the object does not experience any linear acceleration.

2.Rotational Equilibrium: This occurs when the sum of all external torques acting on the body about any axis is zero.

$\sum \vec \tau= \vec0$

Note: Rotational equilibrium ensures that the object does not experience any angular acceleration.

Examples of Rotational Equilibrium : Seesaw ,Balance Scale

Relation Between torque and Angular Acceleration

$\tau_{\text {net }}=\mathrm{I} \alpha$

Note: This equation is valid only for fixed axis.

Rotating Pulley

Angular acceleration for heavy pulley

Friction is present between the string and pulley i.e. There is no relative slipping between string and pulley.

No slipping

$\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {string }}\right)_p=\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\text {pulley }}\right)_p$

$\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{R} \alpha \Rightarrow \quad \alpha=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{R}}$

$\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~g}}{\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2+\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{R}^2}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\frac{\text { Net force along string }}{\left(\text { total mass of blocks }+\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{R}^2}\right)}$

Toppling:

In many situations an external force is applied to a body to cause it to slide along a surface. In certain cases, the body may tip over before sliding. This is known as toppling.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Angular momentum of a Particle : Angular momentum of a body about a given axis is the product of its linear momentum and perpendicular distance of line of action of linear momentum vector from the point of rotation.

Angular momentum = Linear momentum × Perpendicular distance of line of action of momentum from the point of rotation

$\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{mv} \times \mathrm{r} \sin \theta \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~L}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}$

Here$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}=$ angular momentum of a moving particle about point O

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}$ is the is the linear momentum of the particle

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}$ is the position vector of the particle regarding the point.

Unit :  kg – m2/sec

Dimension : [ML2T–1]

Angular momentum is an axial vector and it is also defined as moment of linear momentum.

• If line of motion of a particle passes through point 'O', then angular momentum about point O will be zero.

$\begin{aligned} &(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}})_0=0\\ &\text { Because } r_{\perp}=0 \end{aligned}$

Direction of angular momentum: Determined by Right hand thumb rule

Angular momentum of a rigid body rotating about fixed axis:

$L = I \omega$

Angular momentum of combined rotation and translation

Angular momentum of the body about a point P outside the body is given by,

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_p=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{cm}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_{\mathrm{cm}}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_p=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{cm}} \vec{\omega}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}} \times \mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{cm}}$

Note: Always consider positive and negative sign while calculating these values.

Newton's 2nd Law in Rotation: It states that net external Torque acting on a system about any point O (or axis) is equal to rate of change of angular momentum of system about any point O (or axis).

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad\left(\vec{\tau}_{\text {ext }}\right)_0=\frac{d L_0}{d t} \quad \text { Also, } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_0=\mathrm{I}_0 \vec{\omega} \\ & \text { So, }\left(\vec{\tau}_{\text {ext }}\right)_0=\frac{d\left(I_0 \vec{\omega}\right)}{d t}=I_0 \frac{d \vec{\omega}}{d t}=I_0 \vec{\alpha} \end{aligned}$

$\vec{\tau}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\Delta \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{f}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\mathrm{t}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Conservation of Angular Momentum (COAM): If the resultant external torque acting on a system is zero then the total angular momentum of the system remains constant.

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau}_{\mathrm{cxt}} &= \frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dL}}}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ \text{If } \bar{\tau}_{\mathrm{ext}} &= 0 \Rightarrow \frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dL}}}{\mathrm{dt}} = 0 \\ &\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}} \text{ is constant} \\ &\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{i}}} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{f}}} \end{aligned}$

$I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$

Rotational kinetic Energy:

The energy possessed due to rotational motion of a body is known as rotational kinetic energy.

It is a scalar quantity.

$\mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_2 \mathrm{v}_2^2+\ldots=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{r}_1^2+\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{r}_2^2+\ldots\right) \omega^2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2$

Relation between angular momentum and Rotational kinetic energy:

$\mathrm{KE_{Rotation}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2$

$\mathrm{KE}_{\text {rotation }}=\frac{\mathrm{L}^2}{2 \mathrm{I}}$

Total kinetic energy in combined translation and rotation: If during rotation, the centre of mass of the rigid body undergoes translational motion, it will have both translational and rotational kinetic energy.

$\mathrm{K}_{\text {total }}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MV}_{\mathrm{C}}^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}} \omega^2$

Rotational power: The power associated with the work done by torque acting on a rotating body.

$P_r=\vec{\tau} \cdot \vec{\omega} .$

Work-Energy Theorem in Rotational motion: The change in the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid body equals the work done by external torques exerted on the body. This equation is analogous to equation corresponding to the work-energy theorem applicable for a particle.

Work done by the torque = Change in kinetic energy of rotation

$\mathrm{W}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega_2^2-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega_1^2$
